utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is it that had some matters to raise. Is it you, Mr. Tapuskovic? Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, everyone. It is really I who is going to raise a point; and, if possible, I would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you and the other Judges are aware of the problems that the Defence has in communicating with their client. We have small exchanges during the hearings; however, today, we were told that it was not going to be possible anymore. We were told that by the security because they have to stay in their places next to the accused. In our mind, this could pose a problem in our communication, which is already modest, it has to be admitted, and the Defence needs to bring this problem to your notice so that we can find a solution and redress the problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you mentioned that because that was brought to my attention and the attention of the other Judges just before we entered Court. It is a matter of concern to us because the accused must be able to communicate with his counsel. At the same time, we have to be sensitive to the security concerns. This is a matter that would affect not only this trial. It's a Tribunal-wide matter, and so I intend to take it up along those lines with the President of the Tribunal and the registrar. In the meantime, as an interim measure, I understand that usher will respond to, I presume, a raised hand from the accused, when he has a note, and the usher will traverse the courtroom and collect the note and pass it to you. I would like to think that it shouldn't be beyond our competence to elaborate a more effective and a smoother method; but for the time being, that is what will happen. Well, please have the witness brought, and I must bring to your attention another matter of concern. The direct examination for this witness was four hours and 29 minutes; the cross-examination, four hours and 10 ten minutes; 30 minutes questions by Judges. All told, four and four, eight, a little over nine hours, and we believe that that is much too long. So starting from the next witness the Court will be more rigorous, more stringent in the allocation of time and the observance of that time. The next witness will be three hours, and it will be will be split evenly between the two sides. So the witness now will be re-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Katic, I would like to take you back to a couple of topics and cover them as briefly as and as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I first ask for that brief video film that was shown; P620, I believe it was, that was shown at the end, to be put up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes let that be shown. The Prosecutor will help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's coming, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted -- never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have already seen this, Mr. Katic and last time you spoke about the smoke?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If Mr. Tapuskovic wants to see it again from the beginning, it is very easily done. I make the offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then freeze the movie at the time when we see the smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll start it at the beginning. There are some people talking, then you see the Presidency, and then we'll freeze it when the explosion occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Last time, you gave us your opinion on this, and I don't want to take you back to that. There was also discussion about an artillery projectile. Now, if it weren't for this smoke, if the smoke dispersed, would you be able to tell us more about what happened to the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the smoke dispersed, and if I saw on the building segments of broken facade or wall or that an artillery shell had fallen outside the building, we would see fragments on the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next thing has to do with that order that was invoked several times here, P496. Now, could you please look at the date; and if you can memorise the number, at least try. Look at the heading.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is 7 November 1994, and the number is 2336-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What in your view does this document represent? Look at the format. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In what form?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an acquired information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you in what form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe, Your Honours, you will think it is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But is it a written order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is an order in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at the document P751.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 751.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can, read the beginning of that first sentence and the number -- or rather, read the whole first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Following verbal orders of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, immediately repeat assignment pursuant to my enactment, strictly confidential number 20/15-342, dated 24th November, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you notice anything that could be linked to that order we saw just a moment ago, regarding the documents, the form of the order, or these references to a previous order? Do you see any link?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document has nothing to do with the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at document 533 now -- sorry, P33. It's a Prosecution document. Mr. Katic, you've seen this already. You saw it yesterday. Could you please look again and tell me in which direction is it mentioned here that VRS forces are firing, attacking?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this document, we see that the forces of the army of Republika Srpska are attacking in the area of Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it mentioned anywhere that Miljacka or another area under the command of the BH army is involved?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this letter sent to General Milosevic, we do not see any references to attacks, other than in Debelo Brdo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, it may be premature to ask this question, but I kindly ask you to help us understand where you are taking us by showing these documents. What was the purpose of showing the first two orders? Was that they were very disparate and unlike? Where are we going? Please assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, we are heading in the only possible direction; namely, to establish whether one of the two documents we have seen is a verbal order invoking some other document of I don't know which operation. I'm not going to interpret the documents now, and one written order which has no basis in the documents with which they tried to establish a link. In other words, a link was claimed between two documents which are in no way related. I'm not going to go into their interpretation because that would involve a debate, but what I care about is to show you that those two documents have no obvious link. I can go into interpretation only when the time comes, and I'll tell you in our final brief what I think about it. But I want the witness to note that between one order and the written order there is no link, not in terms of date or the number or the information included in either of them. That's one thing. And related to the second event, it is said here that fire was along Miljacka river and those shells were heading towards town, towards settlements; whereas, it says clearly here that fire was in the area of Debelo Brdo, where artillery attacks also originated, an area held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think it would be very helpful, at least it my understanding of your case, if you would be kind enough to suggest which conclusion you would like the Chamber to draw from showing this evidence to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. Maybe I should answer it now; although, I believe that maybe the Defence is not supposed to reveal everything immediately. But let me say that the document that speaks about a direct order, the phrase is "I hereby order," and we can even ask the witness what was to be done if somebody receives an order saying "I hereby order," and then fails to execute. Now, if a verbal order was given, then what does a written order which is irrevocable in military terms have to do with it? If I went further into those documents, I could make a few more points, but that would take time. I think for the time being this is sufficient. As for the other matter, the fire directed at Debelo Brdo from which artillery attacks were originated is a response, a deserved response; whereas, the Prosecutor claimed that the fire was in the opposite direction, across Miljacka river, at inhabited areas. I'm trying to show that this was a military conflict, fire was from both sides, and even that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina fired more at the town; whereas, the VRS fired across the town at Debelo Brdo. In such a conflict, tragic outcomes are always possible. And as my colleague has just reminded me, these were Prosecution exhibits, and I am entitled to seek additional clarification regarding such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Absolutely. I don't question your right to do so. My only concern is that by the time we get to the end of the case, we might have forgotten the importance of these documents. That's why I think it might be better to make the points while we have the documents on the screen. But let's stop now, and I kindly ask you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now move to Prosecution Exhibit P667. It's a Prosecution exhibit, again, and I don't want to go into all the details here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But could you please tell me, briefly, what is a Bofors gun? What calibre is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is a 20-millimetre gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please look at what it says under item 1 in this order. Item 1.2, could you please read it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediately" --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Those weapons are to be used only if the Muslim attacks are to be repelled."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Could you please look at item 4, the first sentence. Can you just read out the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please be brought up to the screen. That's the second page. "I strictly forbid the use on own initiative of heavy weapons that are located in collection points under UNPROFOR control. Any such removal and use of these weapons, in case of the need, will be requested by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at document 758. This is the document that we received in the course of the examination-in-chief. Are you able to see the date in the letterhead?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The 5th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did you assume your office, the president of the Novo Sarajevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 13th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we just look at it quickly. Item 3 on page 1, could you just read the title.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Accommodation of the population."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: B?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Food supplies."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: C.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it. We should move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, fine. We should not go into all of this. The Prosecution insisted here. I think it's item -- item 6. Could you please look at item 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And since the Prosecutor read out everything, apart from the last sentence, could you please read the last sentence in item 6.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We visited the nunnery" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The last sentence in the first passage, the paragraph under item 6?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. "We informed the Muslims that they would be safe if they were militarily neutral to us, and so far the situation has been good."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the photograph 754, P754, and then I will have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, could you please tell the Judges, first of all, while you were in the trenches, as you recounted to us, you gave us the time-frame work and you told us what you were doing there. You, as a rank-and-file soldier, what could you do on the orders of your superior? What could you fire on at the separation line?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the location where I was deployed as a soldier for around 11 months, I was able to fire only in the direction of Debelo Brdo or at Grbavica where the Republika Srpska army was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell me, since on this photograph you indicated the separation line so precisely here and we already dealt with all this yesterday, what was happening between the warring factions on this separation line, primarily in terms of the positions of the two warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say, and, in fact, I did indicate this with the red line, where the Bosnia-Herzegovina army troops were stationed. Here, on this photograph, they were in building marked as B; and in the Invest Banka building, just opposite, was the Republika Srpska army. And all along the Miljacka, there were positions manned by the BH army; and on the other bank of the Miljacka, there were the troops of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What weapons were used primarily, and what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only infantry weapons were used on both sides, automatic and semi-automatic rifles. It was impossible to use heavy weapons here. Neither side could it that. There were some sporadic exchanges of fire in 1994; and up until the spring of 1995, after the cease-fire was signed in 1994, sometimes you would hear gun-fire in that part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned living beings. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we Serbs use the term, "ziva sila," personnel for the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from those locations that you marked with M and F, now, regarding the street that is just in front of these buildings in this area here, what buildings dominated this area? These buildings are not on this picture, but do you know their names and where they were?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the left of this photograph, there was the assembly hall of the city of Sarajevo. I think it had 22-storeys. The Unis buildings, which were the tallest buildings again to the left of this photograph, just opposite Holiday Inn hotel, they were tall buildings, 20-storeys and 22-storeys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Katic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I would like to thank the Tribunal for allowing me to assist in your endeavours. I would like to thank you, the Prosecution and the Defence, and I would also like to say good-bye to all of you, and to you Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is the next witness, Mr. Tapuskovic? Who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is Dragan Timic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Dragan Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to lead the witness on those basic matters until we get to the main issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, your name is Dragan Simic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, none of the exhibits that you intend to introduce through this witness - and I see, one, two, three, four, five - none of them have been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I actually wanted to ask you right at the beginning, it's just a brief document. I may not even show this document to the witness because it is a very brief document that I was able to translate, and I can in fact tender it through any witness. So we don't really have to interpret it here. It has just a couple of sentences, but it could be quite useful for the Court. And if I am unable to use because of lack of translation, I intend to use only one page of this document. The rest is just some military records, some military documents that have nothing to do with this witness. But if do you not agree, then, I will not tender it, because I can do it through any witness. But this witness was a direct participant in an event that this document pertains to, and he can tell us something about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we'll begin the examination-in-chief, but I'd like to stress, to emphasise that you're obliged to follow the Rules of the Court, and you must have your documents translated. That's an obligation on all parties, not only you. So let us proceed and see whether we can get along without the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I have to tell you something. The Defence is making great efforts to translate all the documents, and I will -- perhaps this will be the last time that I intend to use an untranslated document. But I have to tell you that when we were allotted the time to prepare our 65 ter list of documents and witnesses, we addressed the CLSS, the translation service, with our requests for some documents to be translated, and we were told that none of those documents could be translated before the 1st of June and that they're still working on some documents that we had submitted earlier. We are making great efforts, and I could have had it translated on my own or found somebody to translate it. This is very -- it is very difficulty. I don't have the service at my disposal, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Simic, you were born on the 5th of November, 1968, in Han Pijesak, in the village of Dzimrije?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed elementary and secondary education in the village of Sokolovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you graduated from the secondary school of metal working in 1987?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of 1990, you worked at Unis factory at the tool production plant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you lost your job. You were laid off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges what happened then. How long were you unemployed, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, before 1991, I lost my job. That -- and then in September 1991, I was mobilised into the JNA in Han Pijesak. I was drafted into the 216th Mountain Brigade there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of tasks did you do? What did you do in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in the military police company. I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, who was your direct superior and who did you drive around?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: That was Captain Ljubisa Milic. I drove him around most frequently, and sometimes the brigade command members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 216th Mountain Brigade of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: That was Dragomir Milosevic, who was a colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you drive him around until the conflict broke out, if we can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, where were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was at Lukavica when the conflict broke out. That was on the day when the incident at Dobrovoljacka Street happened, so it was early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you drive to Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: My commander and two other -- other officers, commanding officer officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was Ljubisa Milic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in the days that followed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I spent the days that followed at Lukavica, until the second half of May when the JNA started pulling out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel and witness should make pauses between questions an answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please observe a pause between question and answer to facilitate the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened? You went there at the time of the incident in Dobrovoljacka Street. What happened in the next few days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Again, I drove the officers, as need may be; and, usually, it was my captain, Mr. Misic, until the second half of May. On a certain day in the second half of May, he said that I should take him to Han Pijesak, and he told me that he was to travel to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did he recommend for to you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I asked him what am I to do from then on? And he said you can go home; and if there's a need for you, someone will give you a call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is your house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: My family house is in the village of Dzimrije, and we had another house in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What took place in the next few days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In that month or month and a half, I was with my parents, and there was a family tragedy because my father was killed close to our house on the 30th of June, 1992. He was killed some 2 to 300 metres away from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did that happen? Can you explain to us briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: My mother and father went to fetch some firewood, and my mother noticed a group of people in the forest. All of a sudden they opened fire upon them. My father was killed and my mother, by sheer luck, managed to survive. She came to the house, and she told me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were any other vents important for the few next days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Within the next week, my uncle was killed in the nearby village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please move closer to the microphone because the interpreter is having difficulty hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After a month and a half, during which you were at home and after all those things, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: After all those events and the tragedy we suffered, I reported to Han Pijesak to the military office there, and I was told to go to Lukavica to report to the 1st Romanija Brigade, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, during our examination today, please bear in mind to watch the cursor on the screen. Once it has stopped, then proceed with your answer. Who commanded the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at Lukavica, the 1st Romanija Brigade commander was Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were with the military police. Please wait for me to finish. What were your tasks once in the unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the military police company as a driver, and that was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who were the people that you drove?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Most frequently, it was the military police commander, Ratko Djurkovic, and on occasion some other officers from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did you come to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps staff? Please wait for the transcript, and then proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In early August 1994, I was reassigned to the battalion of the corps police that was stationed at Lukavica; and from there, I was assigned to be a driver and a part of the security detail for the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for me your duties, including the security duty? What were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I was to drive when I was there as a driver, and we had to go close to the enemy lines, were fired upon. As for security, we had to provide physical security for officers or to get stuff for them, if they needed any. And, of course, we had to make sure that we arrived satisfactorily at the place we intended to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get any orders from your commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. All of the orders were received by his assistant, Lieutenant Dobrilovic. He was General Milosevic's assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What, for example, were his orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: He would issue us the task for that day. He would tell us where we were to go. And if he knew, he would let us know how long we would stay there, and then we would usually come back the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Whose driver were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: General Milosevic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simic, wait for the cursor to stop and then start with the reply.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't see it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Go on explaining, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: We received orders from the aide-de-camp, Lieutenant Slavisa Dobrilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These orders were always oral?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would convey those orders to us in the morning or sometimes in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever given any instructions in written form?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Only concerning my specific tasks; where and how I was to drive and how to provide security. My particular tasks en route, and I would given those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I was given those once I was assigned to the unit to be Mr. Milosevic' driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And those were the only written instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were no orders. It was a description of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the command post was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: At Lukavica, in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the 65 ter document 02892. I believe it to be the UNPROFOR map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, on this map, can you indicate where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command was, and please mark it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next to the marking, could you please put the letter K?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were at the command, where were you supposed to be? Where was your workplace?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: There was a room that we used to spend time in, and it was in the other wing, in the building where the corps commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As a driver, were you ever able to attend staff meetings or any other meetings that had to do with the command of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you went out in the field - and we'll discuss this in more detail later - what did the situation look like? Can you explain to us briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When we were in the field, anywhere within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps area, if I was with the command, I was in front of the command and would wait for the general to return, to come back. And when we toured our positions and trenches, then I was beside the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And if there was a forward command post or a trench or anything similar, when were you positioned on such occasions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In front of that particular facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever allowed to attend meetings of staff officers or work meetings between people who were supposed to make decisions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in trenches with him --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Then I was always with him, next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your duty then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: To provide security for the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The place you marked with the letter K, what was the location? Was there anything peculiar about that command post? Perhaps you can tell us which side of the world it was, and what was this command post of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command was in a barracks. If one looked towards Sarajevo, between Sarajevo and the command post, there was Mount Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that elevation, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put the letter M there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other hills nearby?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In this part?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, perhaps in some other direction.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon leaving the barracks, going to the right, one goes to the Nisic plateau and to the left towards Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark those. Please mark the direction of Trnovo, put an arrow there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put the already T there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that direction, were there any elevations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Igman. And the Krupac quarry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The direction you marked, upon leaving the barracks, in the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, what feature, what elevation was there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: There was Krupac held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is Igman there? Mark it, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: One cannot see it here. Somewhere here approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How would you describe the command location? You said that Mojmilo was nearby?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the other side, there was Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was Gavrica Brdo, Gavrica hill?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Gavrica hill is to the left of the road, in the direction of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please indicate that on the map.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it with a G.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is its altitude compared to Mojmilo and Igman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It is quite lower than both Igman and Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where else did you go when going out into the field? Please mark those directions with arrows.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: We went towards the Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please put an arrow to mark the direction.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It is towards Vraca. The road takes you through Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mark it with a N.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And put another arrow for any other directions you were able to take.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put a P there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the direction towards Pale; and in order for to you be able to reach the Nisic plateau, where did you have to go? Perhaps you needn't mark the whole route, but just let us know which direction you had to take.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In order for me to reach the Nisic plateau, I had to go to Pale through Mrkovici, and it was also a difficult area to go through. We were targeted there from Grdonj, and from there we had to go to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put a V, letter V there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you were going towards Nisici, just draw a small arrow to show the direction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What's the distance from Nisici to there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean from Vogosca? Thirty to 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And if you were going towards Ilidza, could you draw an arrow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the distance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Fifteen to 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: From Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put a letter I.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And if you were to go on to Nisic, could you draw the whole -- an arrow the whole way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Not Nisici. To Nedzarici. Leave this line. It doesn't hurt. Draw a line up to Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you must have been able to go further on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was difficult. It was difficult to pass through to the end. It's here up in the middle, Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And why was it difficult?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Because Nedzarici was surrounded on three sides. It was like a dead end of sorts. It was difficult to drive. It was easier to walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe how you guarded Dragomir Milosevic when you were out in the field? Be it in Nisic or in Trnovo, how did you actually serve as his security man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, when we were going towards Trnovo or the Nisic plateau, I had to protect our cars by putting flakjackets in the inside, along the doors. It was a difficult work because we used all sorts of byroads. If we were going through Trnovo, it was rough terrain, very difficult to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain, how often did the general go out into the field, as opposed to staying at his command post in Lukavica? Where did he spend more time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Most of the time he was out in the field. I just remember that for a while in the beginning of August, or maybe September when I arrived, we spent more time in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was quiet. There was a truce, a cease-fire. There was not much activity, so we didn't go out into the field that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what started happening in October?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In October 1994, an offensive began, an offensive of the BH army, in the area of Trnovo and Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the months that followed, where did you spend your time in day-time? Could you describe your average workday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: At that time, in the morning, I would receive orders from my superior for that day. We would go early out into the field, be it towards Trnovo or towards the Nisic plateau, and we would stay there the whole day, until late at night. Since passage was difficult by roads that we normally used, we had to get up very early to get to the Nisic plateau or Trnovo; and when we got there, I would first take the general to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you arrived at a command post, where would you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I would stay outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just remember the pauses. And after the command post, where did the general go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Almost every time he would go to defence lines held by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that when he was on the front line in trenches, you were next to the General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Remember the pauses. Did you hear what he said to the troops when he addressed them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Most often, or rather, constantly, he told them to take care, to be always on the lookout, not to fire without any need, to save their ammunition, because the offensive will be stopped, that they will be successful in defending their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in that area, speaking of the Nisic plateau and Trnovo, but let stay on the Nisic plateau for a while, were there any civilian buildings nearby? Were there any local residents there? What kind of place is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. On the Nisic plateau, there were very few houses and all of them were destroyed. It was practically a roadless area, wooded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were in Trnovo, could you show the Judges where Nisici is and where Trnovo is on this map? Just point it out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Shall I get up? This is the Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the situation in Trnovo? Were there any civilian settlements? Were there any civilians at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In Trnovo itself, yes, there were civilians. There were some on the lines and close to the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And which ethnic group lived there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In Trnovo, you mean? Serbs mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, briefly, how long did this clash between the BH army and the VRS last after starting in October?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Around a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you remember an event from that period in Trnovo, whether there were people who were living there? Did anything stick in your mind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember in November, I had brought the general to Trnovo. People were rallied there. I don't know exactly how many. And when I got out of the car, I found out that they were asking the general to provide transportation so they can move out of Trnovo. That was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: They said - I could hear that myself. I heard the people speak - that it was a very powerful fierce offensive. They were afraid that the BH army would get to Trnovo and pass through, and they remembered year 1992 very vividly when Trnovo was under the BH army. The general addressed them, saying that they should stay, they shouldn't go, that he would do everything to make sure that the lines are secured, and that Trnovo is saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did -- when did this fighting stop?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Sometime in December, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what followed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: From January to May 1995, it was quiet. There was a cease-fire, but even then the roads that I used were targeted, but not so badly as when fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, from end December to May the next year, which positions did the general visit more often?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: We mostly went to the parts of town held by the army of Republika Srpska; that is, Grbavica and Nedzarici. More often than not we would go to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you had to go to Nedzarici, did you again have to go this roundabout way that you marked with arrows?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that the general went to Grbavica and also other points in town that were under the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did he speak to anyone there? Where did he go most often?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Most of the time he went to see troops in trenches. He addressed soldiers, talked to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did he tell them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: His main point he always repeated that they should be on the lookout, be on their guard, never to relax, only to return fire if attacked directly in their trenches, and to fire only at the military target from which they are fired at. And he always said that they must under no circumstances fire at civilians. He always underlined that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, as I heard it then, he told them, "Don't do that, be careful, pay attention, because you hear all the media saying that we target civilians, and you know yourselves it is not true."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he say anything about what they should be protecting more than anything else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, in Grbavica, he said that their families were behind them, their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And on your travels with him, when you must have spent a lot of time together, did you hear him complain of anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, his only complaint was that there was no food. It was difficult to get hold of food. That's the only complaint I heard from the general a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to be the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we both have to make sure that we do things the way I have already described to you. While we're on this topic of visits to the field, how long would he stay there when he went to the command post or to another area? How long would he stay in the field in the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, 15 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where would he go there, and where did he spend most of the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: He would go to the front lines, to see the soldiers, and he would stay there until late in the evening talking to the soldiers, to the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me, since you accompanied him most of the time, based on what I hear from you, what weapons did you carry while performing your duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: A pistol and an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the heavy weapons exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I think this was in 1994. This was when all the heavy weapons had to be pulled out of the vicinity of the town, to an area maybe 20 kilometres around the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty -- Mr. Waespi, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We have switched seats during the break. The mentioning of the heavy weapons exclusion zone reminds me of the topic of the 65 ter summaries. Already, to my surprise, it was stated that this gentleman is not only the driver but also a security detail of the accused, something which wasn't mentioned in the summaries, and now to go into this whole new world of total exclusion zone. And I'm, in fact, not sure whether this gentleman can elaborate much more on this subject. So I just raise it, Mr. President, again, the issue of the 65 ter summaries, and I think you have at one time announced that there will be a ruling on -- on the sufficiency of the 65 ter summaries. It is really, really difficult for to us prepare. We don't have rank. We don't have specific units these gentlemen belong to. Occasionally, we try to get back to the Defence and ask them to tell us more detail, as I did in an e-mail yesterday. Some summaries are inaccurate. One of the witnesses - I think, it is it P53 - we were told he was a soldier. Now is he a captain. So, in fact, we going to the wrong direction when preparing. So I really urge you, Mr. President, to rule that these summaries be more explicit, so we can really prepare for cross-examination. Otherwise - and I use this word in reluctance - it is not fair to the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Ms. Isailovic, dealt with this issue after an agreement. Could she then now deal with it, because we agreed that she should deal with procedural matters. She replied to this letter by Mr. Waespi yesterday and I dealt with other matters, so do you allow her to respond, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, I have not yet sent the letter because I had some problems with my USB stick. I will do that as soon as possible, of course. But since Mr. Waespi is talking about the inappropriateness of our 65 ter summaries, perhaps this would be the right moment to respond. And I will use the same phrase that I wrote in my letter, that I am about to send, but perhaps it would be more efficient to repeat it now. First of all, the Defence is doing its 65 ter summaries in accordance, fully in accordance with the 65 ter G, Rule 65 ter G, which defines the obligation of the Defence in this respect. The Defence is in compliance with its obligations in the interest of safeguarding the interests and rights of the accused, and the Defence has different obligations in this regard than the Prosecution for a very simple reason: In order to safeguard the rights of the accused. In this respect - and I admit this and so does Mr. Tapuskovic - we have tried and we are trying to make the personal information available to the Prosecution, even if the Rules do not oblige us to do so, in order to -- for them to be able to ascertain the battalion, the brigade, where a certain soldier served, or a location where soldiers fought; not the date of birth, because this is not envisaged by the rules. But I do understand the Prosecutor's concerns. They might want to conduct some investigations because this is their job. The Defence is unable to conduct any deeper investigation regarding some Prosecution witnesses, and the Prosecution, on the other hand, is able to do. I, of course, understand this. If I were in Mr. Waespi's shoes, I would do the same thing; but, of course, we have to comply with the rules in and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and they're not there just like that. There is a reason why they are there, because the 65 ter F that stipulates obligations of the Prosecution and 65 ter G that stipulates the obligations of the Defence are different, worded differently. The Chamber will rule on this issue, but I compared the summaries provided to us by the Prosecution, and I really tried to follow the same structure, the quality and quantity of the information contained therein. We even included more information. Because if you look at the Prosecution summaries, you can't even see whether they -- they did not comply with their obligations, and Judge Antonetti was not very happy with Mr. Stamp's work. He was the Prosecutor at that time. But, of course, we were unable to get anything more. We did get the statements because this stems from another obligation of the Prosecution. There is no reciprocity. It is not a symmetrical obligation that would bind the Defence, too. Mr. Tapuskovic and I, we are really sorry, but we're doing our job in accordance with the Rules, and I will send this letter to my learned colleague, perhaps including some more details, and in the belief or giving him my assurances that the Defence will, in future, try and supply more information. But we, for instance, today notified the Prosecution about some information about a witness who will be called soon. This is something that is -- it's a professional courtesy. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Isailovic. If I am to speak on this issue, I make it clear that I am speaking for myself. In the Slobodan Milosevic trial over which I presided for the presentation of the Defence case, the 65 ter summaries submitted by the accused in that case were even slimmer than what has been submitted. I had my legal assistant check this, and she confirmed this. The practice of Chambers in regard to this issue appears to be not consistent, and there hasn't been any ruling on it by the Appeals Chamber, but I come to the issue with a particular doctrinal background. In my view, the rights and obligations of the Prosecution and the Defence are not necessarily symmetrical. They are certainly asymmetrical in certain respects. The Prosecution has certain duties, which do not apply to the Defence; and I believe in relation to disclosure, that issue is very much influenced by the right to silence of the accused. So I knowledge, yes, there is a provision in the Rules for that, but I believe that provision, like all other provisions in any Rule, must be interpreted in light of the relevant provisions of the statute. So, that as far as I'm concerned, I would not be inclined to oblige the Defence to do more that it is doing, but I would ask them in the spirit of cooperation that has existed between the two teams to do as much as they can. And I make it clear that I'm speaking for myself on this issue. Yes. Would you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I can rephrase the question, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you arrived or you became Mr. Dragomir Milosevic's driver when? When did you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In early August 1994. In early August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were the driver. You did not have any rank. What did you see? What did you observe as you travelled around with General Milosevic in the field, and how much attention did you pay to all those extraneous matters; in other words, those matters that were not part of your task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I had precious little time to observe what was happening around me. All I know is I heard either from the soldiers or from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, that's not what I meant. You said that you had a pistol and an infantry weapon. Did you come across any other weapons? What did you observe at the time? You said that you were aware of the total exclusion zone. What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: At the Nisic plateau, I saw some cannons, mortars, and maybe a tank a or two, and I noticed the same thing in the Trnovo sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you went to the positions in Ilidza, Dobrinja, Nedzarici, Grbavica, what did you observe there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Just the troops with infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any weapons anywhere? In some locations, they were in the no combat positions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I did notice that there was something under UNPROFOR control, if I remember correctly. But I don't know where exactly it was. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Could you please tell me, you said that there was this peaceful period and you explained to us where General Milosevic was. How long did this period last, the one that you just described to us? What happened in this period? Were there any events related to military activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The -- do you mean the period from January until spring? If that's what you mean, it was a peaceful period. We didn't travel much. We only went to the parts of the town where Republika Srpska army troops were, and this lull lasted until May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened in May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Fierce attacks were launched from the town, from areas controlled by the BH army, and all the routes that I used to drive the general around were targeted on a daily basis. It was impossible to move on them. I had to take good care of my car. We travelled by night, and the Zlatiste stretch was particularly risky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't save the map. And in the meantime, I did not call up any documents. I don't know if the map that we used to mark -- I don't know if this map is still on the screen. And if it can be given a number, I would like to tender the map, the UNPROFOR map with the markings made by the witness as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a 65 ter document 02930. The witness mentioned Zlatiste, and I would like to have the witness explain some things to me. As I entered the courtroom today, although I did not put this photograph on my initial exhibit list, the -- Mr. Waespi agreed that this photograph, 65 ter 02930, that I could use it. Do I have your approval, too, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the image has been preserved, perhaps we can look at the photograph I have just mentioned. It is a 65 ter document, number 02930. It is somewhat dark. Could we make it a bit brighter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you show to the Chamber where Zlatiste is, since you mentioned it a minute ago? Could you show us that place in the photograph, and please mark it, since I believe you will be able to find it, and with the usher's assistance will be able to mark that spot? Show us Zlatiste, please. Provided you can see it there, could you mark it with a line, please, across the entire area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If one looks closely, and I believe the photograph is excellent in that regard, can you also see the road there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that line, well, please put a Z close to it first.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the middle of the line, can you put -- make another line, but the question first. Can you mark Debelo Brdo on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please put a line there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: By which letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Letter D.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you connect the end of the line, or rather, the beginning, as you mark -- as you marked it? Can you connect the locations of Zlatiste and Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The area you marked with the third line, put a letter L there, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the VRS positions were? Just indicate it to us, and do not enter any markings as of yet. Were they at the first line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The VRS positions were at the front line close to the road, which is the first line I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the area between the VRS positions and Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No one controlled that area. It was like a buffer zone, a no man's land. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was at Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where a tower is? There was a mention of a tower close to the VRS positions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Zlatiste tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put an M there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During that May, what was important about the tower?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The lines, the positions followed the road I mentioned and near the tower; therefore, the tower was constantly exposed to the fire from Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did the road go? The road across Zlatiste, where did it go compared to the elevation where the tower was, if we are looking at Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Looking from Lukavica, it went towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Looking from the line that you marked and towards the spot where you said the tower was, where did the road go compared to the tower?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean the Zlatiste tower?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: To the right-hand side there was a forest, and the road went across the positions I indicated and via Zlatiste, where I put the Z.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From that road, there was no open view of the city of Sarajevo from behind the hill where the tower was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was difficult. One could only see the parts of the city across the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The witness gave the answer, but it was clearly leading in this question, that there was no view; and, in fact, it doesn't reflect the evidence on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was a leading question. You must avoid leading questions, Mr. Tapuskovic. Evidence elicited by leading questions has no value.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with that practice. It applies to my legal system as well, and leading questions are not permitted, although there is no cross-examination. Therefore, I accept your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, tell me this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a suggestion; it's a ruling. I don't make suggestions; I give rulings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was a matter of interpretation or a poor choice of wording. I know that you rule on matters, and it is fully correct. I may not pose leading questions. Your assessment was a correct one, and I have tried my entire career not to put leading questions because in our system, one is not allowed to put leading questions, and I believe it to be a weakness, since we have no cross-examination at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How can you reach Zlatiste? From what direction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please put an arrow at the beginning of the line you entered first.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the other end of that line, where does the road go from there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Towards Pale. Trebevic-Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. On the other end of the line, please put another arrow there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The first arrow should be marked with a L; the other arrow with a P.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is the distance concerning the first line you marked? How large or long is the area as Zlatiste, as you marked it up to the letter Z?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Some 300 to 350 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What begins there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Upon leaving Lukavica, and if one has passed the Zlatiste tower, that part of the road, that stretch of 300 metres begins the one that was open to fire. There was the army there; and once you've passed the 300 or 350 metre, one enters a dense forest on the right-hand sides and the road goes on to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long is the stretch through the forest?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Around ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When driving through the forest, what did you usually come across?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Across the soldiers that were in the trenches there, close to the road, on one part of that leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the general issue any orders when travelling that stretch of the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard him order anything. If sometimes we stopped, that would only be -- that was only to greet the soldiers, but I never heard him issue any orders there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain. How come he didn't issue any orders there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The forest was dense, century old trees, and one couldn't see anything. The confrontation line was on both sides of the forest; but from the forest itself, one cannot see anything. You can only see the trees before you. Probably for that reason he didn't need to stop there frequently or at least as frequently as he did at the Nisic plateau and Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. So he was going through that forest in order to get where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: To Pale. Once out of the forest, you have some 20 kilometres left to Pale, from Zlastiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where would he go from there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: If we were going towards the Nisic plateau, we went towards Vogosca; and then we would turn to the Nisic plateau via certain places that we had to go through, for example, Derventa, Somborac, Hresca, and then we would start encountering problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard about that from other witnesses. The distance between Zlatiste and Debelo Brdo, what is it and how far is it from one another? I don't think I asked you about that yet. What is the distance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: About 300 metres more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From Zlatiste, that you had marked with the first line, what can you see?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Only the parts of the city that were across the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask that this photograph be assigned as a number, and be given a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you said that in May there were certain events that you described at Zlatiste. What did it look like? How many days did it last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It began in early May. I don't remember the exact date. But in mid-May, by that time, the road was already cut off, the road between Lukavica, Trebevic, and Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in mid-May, which VRS position was the most forward?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about Zlatiste? Zlatiste. They targeted that part the most from Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And during those days, where was General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: He usually came to the observation post that was just above Zlatiste, above the road, a few metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we could give the witness a clean sheet of paper for him to be able to draw a couple of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The usher will hand him a clean sheet of paper. And I take the opportunity to say to the accused, Mr. Milosevic, you should not feel inhibited by the new procedure for to you communicate with your counsel because I notice, and it has been observed by my colleagues, that no note has been passed. We have the usher available to pass whatever notes you have to your counsel. You need only raise your hand, and the usher will collect your note and pass it to your counsel. So don't feel inhibited. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understood. There was no need for me to pass any papers so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I recall correctly, this was assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What? Yes. We assigned an exhibit number. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you draw the part of the road that you had initially marked on the photograph, at least approximately? Can you depict it on the sheet of paper before you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. At the beginning of those two lines, could you show where Lukavica is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When -- at which point on that road do you begin to see Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Next to a forest there, next to a -- outside a tower in Zlastiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the Zlatiste tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it with a K, for Kula tower.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in those days, how many times was General Milosevic on this road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: We went to that observation point, I believe, every day for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to General Milosevic on that road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: He was wounded. That was in mid-May. I don't recall the exact date. He was wounded on the observation point which was to the right from the road, if you are going from Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw the place where that observation point was relative to this tower? How far was it from the tower and on which side of the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the observation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put an S there.
