utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did it look like, this observation point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was dug into the ground, and on the outside it was boarded up. And there were -- it was boarded up on top as well and covered with soil. It was on the right-hand side of the road, if you are going from Lukavica, just a couple of metres --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. It was dug into the ground. But if we are looking at the road, was it level with the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was just a couple of metres above the road, but it was dug half a metre or maybe one metre into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just wait a minute. Just wait for the question, please. Who was at that moment inside the tower, or rather, in the observation point when he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The general and the staff officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where were you? Show us the place where you were.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In the communicating trench, outside the observation tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Outside, meaning in front?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Behind. Behind, next to the road, behind the observation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark the location where you were standing with the letter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And apart from the staff officers at the observation post, where were the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The soldiers were on the road, along the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you put in this -- this kind of line?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just a moment, Judge Harhoff has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have lost my orientation on your drawing. Can you please indicate where north is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you put an arrow, pointing towards the north, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I have made a mistake. The first question I should have asked you is: What can you actually see from the observation post from that point where you actually look?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: You can see Kovacici, parts of the town, the brickworks, Pofalici, all the way down to the Miljacka, Hum, and Zuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what direction is it in terms of points of the compass, north, south, east?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it's in a northerly direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please draw a line from the observation post.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please mark it with F.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can mark it with N for north, but F is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Harhoff, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. I understood the drawing to indicate that the direction of the road was coming from Lukavica, which is the arrow at the bottom of the screen; is that correct? So you're coming from Lukavica, moving east on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you have the city down on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the left, to the left, from the direction of Lukavica. Perhaps the witness could just mark where Pale is, in what direction. And now the witness can perhaps give us an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you're going in the direction from Lukavica, could you please mark that with an L. So the first arrow is marked with an L. Could you then mark a P the letter up -- the arrow up there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if you're going from Lukavica, where is Sarajevo now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: To the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If anything is not clear yet, I can do whatever I can to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But now we have come to this broken line here. So the soldiers were there, and you said that they were there where the broken line is. Why is the broken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was the defence of Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who had a better line of sight towards Sarajevo, the soldiers or the staff officers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The staff officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were there in those moments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened there on one -- one day, as you just told us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In mid-May, the general was wounded. I don't recall the exact date, but he was wounded at the observation post. He was hit -- the observation post was hit from the direction of the town, maybe Pofalici, I don't know exactly, and the general was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of a round hit the observation post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I learned later, about an hour or two later, that it was hit by a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, an officer explained that on the basis of the fragments that remained after the shell hit the observation post, that it was actually a tank shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you first pay attention to from the position where you were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: When the observation post was hit, some ten seconds later, I rushed inside. I saw all of them there. There was smoke, there was dust, and there was blood on the general's face. I carried him out. There another building next to the observation post. There was the medical service there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: So this is where the medical station was. I brought him there, he was given treatment for 20 to 30 minutes, and they were telling him that he had to go to hospital. He refused to go, and then they treated this injury that he had. It was an eye injury, a head injury, in other words. And then after some 60 minutes, he was back at the observation post. That was all on the same day, with a bandage around his head and a patch on his eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Until late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else injured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't remember. I knew those people, but I don't remember their names now. One of the soldiers had sustained serious injuries, and some officers were also hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me from those positions where you were -- I have to repeat this question. From the observation post and from the positions manned by the soldiers along the road, how well could you see the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As rightly observed by Mr. Tapuskovic, the questions have been asked and answered before, and the second time the witness made the distinction. And, in fact, the question was distinguished into what the soldiers saw and what the observation point was able to look at. So to group now those two issues into one question is not helpful, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. My question was -- my question was what he could see. Who had the better line of sight and he replied, but now I'm asking him what he could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let us ask him that. From the observation post, what could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just parts of the town across the Miljacka, Pofalici, Kosevo, those parts of the town from the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And from the positions manned [Realtime transcript read in error "marked"] by the soldiers on the road, what could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even less from there, because the observation post was about a couple of metres higher than the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My question should have read from the positions "manned" by the soldiers. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a question that calls for a clarification. I can see the sketch that you drew for us. The upper part that goes from Lukavica to Pale, I can see the observation post. But can you please tell me where exactly is the confrontation line? In other words, can you please tell me where the BH army lines would be on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is Debelo Brdo, the positions at Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are the BH army positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Debelo Brdo to the road, there were skirmishes there, exchanges of fire between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gist of my question is: I want to see where the confrontation line was in relation to the town of Sarajevo itself. And, also, in order to be able to understand where fire was opened, and from which position this observation post was targeted and hit, could you please clarify that, or do you believe that you've clarified everything that you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The observation post was hit from the direction of Pofalici. This is the direction that I marked with F. So this was the direction from which the observation post was hit. That's the direction of Pofalici, Kosevo, and the brickworks. And Debelo Brdo, this is where the BH army had its positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to clarify this issue that Judge Mindua has insisted on, I first have to complete this sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could you, Witness, please mark the road, the length of the road, and indicate the length from which the Republika Srpska army was operating. How -- what length would that be approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: About 350 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to remark that this is actually much easier to understand if you put this sketch in this position horizontally, and could this please be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just -- let us just determine where the shell had come from, the direction from which the shell had come?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Kosevo, this is the line that I drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this to be admitted into evidence. Could this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I was just considering that the last X that he put, to denote the direction from which a shell came, perhaps something should be there to say that this is what it means, because it is really just a X. When we come to review the evidence, it would be useful to have something there to say what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're right. That's exactly what my colleague suggested. Let him now just draw a line from the direction of Sarajevo -- or rather, an arrow. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it with R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness testified he believed it came from Pofalici, so perhaps a P for Pofalici would make a word record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, then. P for Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Simic, you marked Debelo Brdo. How far are Pofalici behind that red circle that you drew in response to Judge Mindua's question? How far from there was it to Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: A kilometre or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we save this drawing as a Defence exhibit now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order for the issue that Judge Mindua insisted on to be clear, we have to have back the photograph 02930. That's a 65 ter number. We must have it back and look at it again, but I would like a clear one, clear of markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, now could you draw a line to show us where the positions of the VRS were. Please draw a line.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't. I don't have a pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please mark it with an S.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now draw a line to show where the BH army was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were those the separation lines, the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This area in between, what about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was empty; there was nothing. It was like a buffer zone, a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So fire came from those two lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark the second line, the BH army line, with a word A -- with a letter A?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you just tell the Judges whether these houses we see there existed at the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this photograph as well as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what happened in the days that followed? General Milosevic was wounded. What happened between the two sides in the days that followed, that May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In the days that followed, intensive fighting continued, all the way until the end of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've now come to the point where that brief document becomes relevant, the one for which I don't have a translation which is only half a page. A document that is ease to interpret, and that I would like it present to this witness. I suppose the Prosecution already has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's proceed. Let's see whether we can get along with it, and whether there is any prejudice to the Prosecution. So let it be placed then on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-3189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We have received seven, eight different documents, and I see it now on display. I really do not understand why, if only one very short document, is it used with this witness. It can be translated. In fact, I did offer to the Defence on Friday that we can translate any documents they -- they indicate to us, and we are happy to do that. And it's just not useful now for everybody in the courtroom who doesn't speak Serbo-Croatian in order to be faced with this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let us proceed with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you read the heading and this document and tell the Court whether the document reflects what happened to General Dragomir Milosevic at that observation point. Can you read it aloud?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: "Certificate." "Certificate, to the effect that" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't read it exactly the way it was written.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: "Certificate, to certify that Dragomir, son of Milorad Milosevic, Major-General, serving at military post box 7598 Sarajevo, was wounded on 17 May, 1995, in the course of combat activities on the Bosut installation in the broader area of Zlatiste. He was wounded as a result of a direct hit from a tank gun on the structured observation post, in which the aforementioned person was leading combat activities. As a result of the explosion and shell fragments, he sustained a serious injury to his right eye."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document, dated 28th August, reflect what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we're on that subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're now 15 minutes beyond the hour and a half that was allotted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best to finish very soon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But you could bypass a document like this. Its relevance, it appears to me, is questionable. Let's move on. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But since we're on the document, can it be reflected on the record that it dates, 1996, if I see that correctly, 28th August 1996. And just to who signed the document, so it -- we have a meaningful record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it a post-dated document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I can tell you is this: This is just an introduction. This document is accompanied by medical documentation. In order to exercise certain rights, later, this document was issued. As for the medical file accompanying this document, I will try to have it translated and ask translators to do it myself. This is followed by the medical file opened from the moment when he reported for treatment. This document alone, without the medical file, does not have great value, but the medical file exists. And it confirms, indeed, all of this, and it is very clear on all matters that are relevant to you. As for the witness, I just wanted to take the witness back to that date. He said he didn't remember it very well and I accept that, and I also accept that this is of no great probative value. It is not post-dated so much, as it was issued on the basis of an earlier medical file. The medical file is self-explanatory, and it was drafted by the teams who treated Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would be the relevance to the injury to Mr. Milosevic in relation to the charges in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among other things, although this might evolve into a legal issue later, this witness could tell us when the accused went to receive treatment and for how long he was absent from the separation line, and how long he was in treatment. And there are a couple of more questions that he could answer to show that after a while, General Milosevic had to leave and to stay in Belgrade for treatment for about a month before returning to the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just try to explain one more thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. The explanation we find is sufficient, so move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, could you tell us briefly about the period of time that followed? What happened after the month of May? What followed in May, June, July, all the way up to August? If you can only be very brief.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: In mid-June 1995, offensives against Trnovo and the Nisic plateau started. They lasted for about 40, 45 days, all the way up to the beginning of August. For the duration of those offensives, we were in the field daily. I would take the general every day to Nisic or Trnovo. At any rate, he was outside the corps command. However, his eye, where he sustained the injury, was giving him more and more trouble, and the infection spread to the other eye. So sometime in the beginning of August, I took him by car to Belgrade to be admitted into a hospital. When I came back home, it was sometime in the first half of September. I went home to my mother's house, and a month later I was told to pick up the general at Han Pijesak, which I did, and drove the general back to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So how long was he absent from the combat positions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: About a month, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you collect him, and where did you take him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I pick the him up at the barracks in Han Pijesak, and from there I drove him to Lukavica. The corps command building was damaged by shelling. It was unusable, and from there I took him to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So when he came back, what had happened to the command post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The barracks where the command was situated was destroyed by shelling -- sorry, by NATO air-strikes. It was already evacuated. It was not completely destroyed, but it was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I think we have two or three minutes before the break. I think we should take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could take good use of these two minutes, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you just before the break. The first one relates to the function of your superior, Captain Ljubisa Milic. I think it was in 1991 or 1992. Can you tell what his job was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Commander Ljubisa Milic was the commander of the police company, all the way up to May 1992. Sometime in May 1992, I took him to Han Pijesak and he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that was the military police company within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you remind us, again, of the name of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: 216th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Commanded by Dragomir Milosevic, at that time a colonel?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, at that time, he had a military police company at his disposition, and just quickly turning to 1994, 1995. There was also a military police unit at the disposition of now the corps commander, Dragomir Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think it's a battalion, not just a company, a whole battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct. It was a battalion, MP battalion, within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the commander after that military police battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, the commander was Vuko Cvoro. I believe he was a captain, maybe a major. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: A competent officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The same day that I arrived at the battalion, of the military police in Lukavica, I was assigned to be the driver of the corps commander. So I met with Cvoro very rarely, because we had our own aide-de-camp who was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the question you asked, because it is not reflected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Whether he was a competent officer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is not reflected in the transcript. We have two answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe you answered the question. You only had minimal contact with this gentleman, the commander of the military police battalion, so you can't really talk much about this -- this commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, we take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, let's talk about a couple of other persons you mentioned this morning. The first gentleman you mentioned was a Lieutenant Dobrilovic, and I believe you said he was Dragomir Milosevic's assistant or aide-de-camp, ADC; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe it was him who gave you your orders for the day, your assignments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Apart from that, what general role did Lieutenant Dobrilovic have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Dobrilovic had the role of issuing us with our daily tasks and passing on orders which he had probably received from the commander. As for the rest, I don't know what else it was that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But he wouldn't accompany you and the commander on your trips to the field?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no. Or very seldom. On occasion, we would spend a few days at a time at the forward command post; and as far as I can remember, he stayed with us on two or three occasions, provided it was planned for to us stay there for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So there were instances where you would spend several days outside of Lukavica without returning in the evenings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did the commander, General Milosevic, keep abreast of what was happening at Lukavica headquarters during these absences?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I wasn't in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did -- do you know Mr. Miljevac, who was a major, an operations officer within the SRK Corps Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would he accompany sometimes the commander with or without you to trips on to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He as well as some other staff officers from the corps command would go in the field with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of some of these other staff officers from the corps who would go in the field with the commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't recall any specific names, but I do remember their ranks. For the most part, these were colonels, lieutenant-colonels, and higher ranking officers who worked at the corps command, of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you don't recall their names, do you recall their functions within the Corps Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone specific for the Corps Staff. I know that the security part was representative, but I don't know about anything else. I was in a different room in a different wing of the building when I spent my time there. The commander was in the other part of the building. I knew Miljevac by chance because he is a distant cousin of mine on my mother's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let talk a little bit about these visits to the front lines, as you have explained to us this morning. You told us, I think on page 28, that you would go into the command post of, I assume, one of the subordinate brigades; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you personally stay at the car, or would you follow the commander when he goes on to one of these brigade commands?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: When I was alone, when there were no colleagues of mine, when there were three of us, if I was driving, I usually stayed in the car. However, if I was guarding the general, then I would escort him all the way to the entrance of the command or to the entrance of a facility, and I would stay in front during the time of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you wouldn't go inside the command post, but you would stay outside providing security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you were out in the field accompanying your commander, providing security, there was another driver then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Not always. We would leave the car either in front of the command or at the point that we were able to reach by car; and from that moment on, we would leave. I would leave with the general. If there was no other driver, I would have to guard him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Leaving the car alone, basically?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Either in front of the command or at the nearest point of approach. If we were supposed to leave the car by itself, we would usually get a soldier either from the command post or the brigade command within the area of responsibility, in order to stay by the vehicle and guard it. Sometimes even as many as two would guard the vehicle. We never left the car alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Incidentally, what kind of cars did you use? Was it always the same, or were there different cars?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Two vehicles: A passenger car and an off-road one, depending on the type of terrain. Depending on that, we would choose which vehicle to use on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us the makes of the passenger car and the off-road car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Passenger because was a Peugeot, and the off-road one was with a Jeep of sorts. I think it was a Toyota.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you or the general have a Puch as well, P-u-c-h?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: We only got the Puch in 1995, towards the end, when the Peugeot was destroyed. It was hit by a shell; and after that, we were given a Puch. I believe it was sometime in 1995. It was a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give us the licence plates of those three cars: The Peugeot, the Toyota, and the Puch. It was a long time ago. But perhaps since you were driving these cars all the time, you might remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. The only thing I can remember is that the plates were military, that they belonged to the VRS, but I can't recall the numbers or the letters. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you're going, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the next question might be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you keep vehicle logs of your trips to the front lines? Did you fill in at the end of each trip where you went to and, you know, what kind of fuel you would spend, when returning to fill up the car? Did you keep that kind of record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where would these records be right now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. After the war I started working, and I can't tell you anything about such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But there is a record, if it still exists, of every single trip you would have made with General Milosevic during the time you were his driver?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We can move on to next issue, unless you have a question, Judge Harhoff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you finishing with this subject of the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then what was the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, we heard a couple of testimonies from Mr. Veljovic and from this witness as well about various trips to certain headquarters and other locations interesting locations. And if we had the vehicle logs, that would be a way to ascertain the credibility of the witnesses and, indeed, get a record of the track, the command of the SRK would follow. Vehicles logs proved invaluable in other cases. Less in this case, but it still prove a great record. And if the Defence, perhaps through another witness, would furnish these vehicle logs, that would be a good way to corroborate some of these, I would say, unsupported allegations that their witnesses are saying. I'm not saying they are wrong. I'm just saying it would be interesting to see the actual vehicle logs, detailing where the SRK commander went to on any given day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But are you disputing the fact that General Milosevic was regularly, frequently in the field, or are you questioning the frequency of his visits, or what is the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not at all. But it is an additional fact for the Prosecution to assess the evidence in its all. There are couple of points where we think General Milosevic has been and for which we don't have independent corroboration, and maybe the vehicle logs would ascertain that. And if the gentleman had the vehicle log with him today, and there was no reason for him to do that, of course, we would be able to go to a specific entry on a specific day and figure out what happened. That's the general purpose. But the Prosecution doesn't dispute, because we have heard it for several witnesses that the general Milosevic went to the front lines, and I'm going to follow-up on exactly this issue right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, during a couple of these visits, or I take the majority of them, you said he has met -- the general has met with soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you told us that he would be talking to them, and they would engage in conversations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But he would stay in the trenches briefly only with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would he also talk to officers, to commanders, in your presence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. Not in the car either. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, from the conversations you might have overheard between the commander and the soldier, what was your impression about the command style of the general Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: My impression was often that he talked to the soldiers as if we were talking to his own children. Every time he would go to see them in the trenches, he would, "Take care of yourselves, be on guard, observe," and this what he often said when I was close to him and when I was able to hear what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you get an impression that he was respected by his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you encounter any instances during the time you accompanied him that a soldier would disobey to any orders of General Milosevic or act in disrespect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I never heard him issue any orders, but I never saw any soldier being disobedient or anyone who would treat the general with disrespect. It never happened in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to a very, very brief issue. The Defence mentioned that the TEZ, total exclusion zone, which prohibited to have heavy weapon within a certain range, 20 kilometres. Do you remember having been asked about that this morning?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what triggered the imposition of that total exclusion zone? Why did the international community start to talk to the two warring factions and try to get the heavy weapons out of Sarajevo? Do you know which event triggered that agreement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know much about it. But as for the pullout of the heavy pieces, I was told stories by other soldiers. They told me how difficult it was to pull those weapons out. That's how I learned that they were supposed to take heavy weaponry out. I discussed that with the soldiers who were involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did these soldiers also tell you that on the 5th of February, 1995, there was a shelling -- 1994, there was a shelling at the marketplace in Sarajevo which caused 64 casualties among civilians of more than 100 people, and this was, in fact, what triggered all the negotiations to have the heavy weapons moved out of Sarajevo? Did you hear about that as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard that through the media. The soldiers that I talked to and I just mentioned a minute ago never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you heard about this incident from the media?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: From the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of media would you consult?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Usually, I listened to the radio in the car. Depending on the area, we would try and locate a radio stations, so we listened to Radio Sarajevo or any other station that we could listen to. I don't know what their names were at the time. I guess there was Radio Republika Srpska as well. Depending on the terrain, we listened to whatever radio station we could tune in to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by "we," you mean Commander Dragomir Milosevic when he was driving with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. Dragomir Milosevic wasn't there in earlier 1994. I think you said February. No, no. When the general drove in the car with me, we also listened to the radio, irrespective of what the radio station was and, as I said, depending on the area we were at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the radio reporting about when you were listening to the radio, if you recall after such a long time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I really can't recall. It's been more than ten years. I was young at the time, and I preferred to listen to some music in the car. I didn't like listening to the news much, unless they were on once I would turn the radio on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on to a few other issues. The first one relates to Debelo Brdo, and I believe you mentioned that the ABiH hold or held Debelo Brdo at that time. Do you remember having said that? Do you also remember that there was, in fact, an UNPROFOR observation point on top of Debelo Brdo, and that the ABiH had positions which were lower to that top.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember there was some structures on Debelo Brdo; but I also know that every day when we were passing, there were combat activities and there was fire from Debelo Brdo in the direction of Zlastiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was: Do you know that there was an UNPROFOR observation point on top of Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember for sure. I believe there was some sort of observation post, some sort of structure on Debelo Brdo. I think it could have been UNPROFOR. At any rate, it was an international force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How do you know there were ABiH forces at Debelo Brdo? Did you visit these regions during the relevant time-period, or did somebody else tell you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were there in their positions on the road told me. At Zlatiste, they would tell me where the fire is coming from currently, that I have to pass through quickly, and with my headlights off. Once, I even stopped specifically to ask them, and the soldiers who were there in their positions on the line at Zlatiste by the road told me to -- what to watch out for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So these soldiers from the SRK had some information about where the ABiH positions were, which they relayed then to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: They would just tell me from where fire was coming at them, from the Debelo Brdo; but where exactly, I didn't know. They just explained to me from which direction fire was coming from. They said it was Debelo Brdo, and they told me to be careful to watch out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, in fact, these soldiers had some knowledge about what was happening in front of them, as they are supposed to as good soldiers. They weren't just sitting in the woods being able to see nothing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they knew it, but there was shooting; and when I talked to those soldiers, they told me the fire was constant against them. On the left-hand side, when you go from Lukavica to the left of the road, there was soldiers in that section of the road, soldiers of the VRS, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We have seen that. That was Exhibit D209. I believe you indicated in a dotted line where the soldiers were located facing Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I'd like to show that photo which we used with Witness Veljovic to this witness. I think it's one of the positions this gentleman might be remember. It's not on my list of exhibits to be used with this witness, but I ask for your leave to do that because I couldn't anticipate that this witness would talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If Prosecution Exhibit 749 be retrieved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while that is being done, you said, in relation to May 1995, you went with the general, General Milosevic, a number of times to that observation point at Zlatiste. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three times before he was wounded, we are at the observation post at Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, if you could look at your screen in front of you. Is that one of the positions alongside Lukavica-Pale road, which would be manned by the SRK soldiers? You can see woods left and right, and you can see one of these dirt, small dirt hills just in front of this person. Is that one of the points alongside the Pale-Lukavica road that you might recall from that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I don't see the road here. If I could see the road, then I could explain. But I can't locate it here, and I cannot even understand from which side this was photographed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I suggest to you that this -- this picture was taken just a couple of metres besides the Lukavica-Pale road, and that can you see on your left side the beginning of Debelo Brdo, would that assist you in determining where this location was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet. To say what, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe Mr. Waespi should not testify himself. If he said if the road were just a couple of metres from this point, would that ring true. Mr. Waespi is suggesting that only a few metres from here, there is the road. On what basis? If the -- what the witness said was if I could locate the road here, then I could explain. We cannot say -- I mean, I don't see on which basis anyone can say that just a few metres behind this man the road runs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just make one small point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is cross-examination. I can put to the witness a proposition for I which I have credible basis, and this is -- this photo was taken alongside the Pale-Lukavica road, and the witness can accept it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're quite right. Yes. In cross-examination, of course, you can do that. I was just wondering whether can you take it any further. But let us hear from him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if I suggest to you that this photo was taken alongside the Lukavica-Pale road, just a couple of metres above, because there were dominant positions, just where Debelo Brdo starts to rise, would you accept that, and would that be one of the positions you and the soldiers alongside the road might have looked at in 1994/1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot orient myself, and I cannot understand from which spot this could have been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. But you testified before the break that from the vantage point at Zlatiste, you could see part of Kosevo where the stadium was, where the hospital was, Pofalici, and anything north of the Miljacka river. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Across Miljacka river, towards Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's exactly the location you can see in this photo. Would you agree at least with that proposition? You see the Kosevo area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I really cannot recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you see the Kosevo stadium, football stadium? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you take a pen, please, and circle it around so we can orient ourselves and you as well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Can we enlarge this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAEPSI
utterances.text: That's probably possible, Mr. Registrar. Just the part above the head of the person we see in the forefront. You must take off his pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if you can stop marking right now. Mr. Simic, does it help you now to mark the Kosevo football stadium?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us where the hospital was, the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I think it's to the right of the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. And just a last point. The Miljacka river would be approximately where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Shall I mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you mentioned Pofalici. I know it's probably not on here, but can you tell us, approximately, the direction of where Pofalici would be located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Now, to have it as a meaningful exhibit, can you please have the letter P above for Pofalici, above the arrow you were drawing last.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The letter M for Miljacka river, alongside the indication where the river is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The letter K for the Kosevo football stadium.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, finally, letter H for the English hospital of where you say, approximately, the hospital was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as an exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P759, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Going back to the point we were about to develop when we started to look at this exhibit, Mr. Simic. You said that you would drive General Milosevic up to that observation point at Zlatiste in May 1995. What time in the morning would you leave, and what time in the evening would you return?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: We went early, maybe around 8.00 a.m., and sometimes we would go back during the day, and then go to the observation post in the evening. That was in the month of May, when the general was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At what time in the evening would you be at the observation point?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Because at the observation post, while there was daylight, they would be inside the observation post; and then next to it, there was another structure where they would spend time until dark -- until dark, when we could safely return to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you would return to the command when it was already dark?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how was the city observed from that observation point, if you know, when it was already dark?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: When it was dark, the officers were no longer in the observation post but in the structure, the brick structure that was next to the observation post; and then after dark, they would go back to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, my question: When it was dark in Sarajevo, how were these officers or whoever observed the city able to observe the city, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone actually observed the town during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to a different subject, and that is the wounding of General Milosevic and his trip to Belgrade. The way I understand your evidence of this morning is you actually accompanied General Milosevic, you drove him to Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, approximately, or perhaps you even know a precise date, when was it that you accompanied the general?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was in the first half of August, but I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So between the 17th of May, when we know he was injured, and this first half of August, General Milosevic would continue to exercise his function as the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did you drive the general to Belgrade? Which route did you take?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Lukavica-Han Pijesak-Zvornik, and that's where we crossed the boarder and then we went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell a little bit about this border control. Did you have to show, you know, an ID, or how did that occur?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had to have our personal ID. I, as a driver, had it to have a driver's licence, the travel order for the car, and the authorisation to cross into Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who issued that authorisation to cross into Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: A service at the Main Staff. For a while, they were issuing such authorisations; and, for a while, you could get it at the command corps, too. But, mostly, it was done by this service at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in Belgrade, where did you drive the general to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I brought the general to the Slavija hotel. There his family took him in. I don't know what happened after that. I went back home, and I spent sometime with my mother in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you brought the general to Belgrade and you, basically, immediately returned back -- back home.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't know what he was doing, with whom he was meeting during his trip in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. The entire time, while the general was there, I was with my mother in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then, I believe, you were told that you can pick up the general from Han Pijesak, is that correct, sometime in September?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, again, if you recall, approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: It was in early September. I don't know exactly when it was, but it was in September. I came to Han Pijesak, and I waited in the barracks in Han Pijesak for the general to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he talk to you when he -- when you picked him up at Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: We talked very seldom, and I don't recall any conversation. I just asked him what the situation was, what his health state was, how -- how he was at the time, how -- what was the surgery like, and he said, "Well I'm fine now. Everything is fine." That was the gist of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And going now from the specifics of this trip back to a general question. Because you just said we talked very seldom, is it also true when you were driving him around that you would hardly go into specifics about what his job was, perhaps personal items?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't talk about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us about these various trips to the command, to the brigades. Did you also accompany him when he would meet with people from the Serb Sarajevo municipal leaders in Vogosca? Do you remember driving him to meetings in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: I drove the general to the municipal halls, sometimes in Vogosca, sometimes in Ilijas, Pale. And I would always stay in front of the municipal hall if I was on the security detail. And if I was just driving, I would there around the car, near the municipal hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you would not follow him into the municipal hall. You would not know whom he would meet there inside the hall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic,that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to thank all of you present here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness is Mr. Sinisa Krsman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may be seated. And you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would like to ask you during your testimony to pay attention to the fact that we really have to speak slowly, and could you please focus on the cursor on the monitor and only start speaking when it stops moving, so that we don't have what we call overlap and so that we can deal with all the issues in the examination as quickly as possible. Thank you. Could you please the Judges first your full name?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: My name is Sinisa Krsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To move quickly through those preliminary issues, you were born on the 17th of December, 1961?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in Sarajevo, Centar municipality, in Zabradze neighbourhood, in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from secondary school in 1970 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1980.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were employed in UPI, it's a company, as a salesperson from 1984 until the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were a salesperson all the time?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would first like to show you a map. That's 65 ter document 27228 -- 2782. Well, you can see this map here in front of you. Could you please show where you lived and the place where you were born?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I can show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the northern section of the map be enlarged a little bit and scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show the location of your house?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I can show it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please mark it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: If we could have the map enlarge as little bit, I can pinpoint the very house. My house is right here where it says Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not marked. Could you please mark it with the letter K.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But could you please tell the Judges, have you already testified by the ICTY, just so that the Judges know?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I testified before this Tribunal in the Stanislav Galic case, and last year I testified in the case against Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at all deal with this map here?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: At that time, we didn't use this map. Other maps were used, and they were not as detailed as this on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you now please show the spot where you worked where your company was at the time when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: My first -- the first place where I worked was at Skenderija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, at the time when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, my workplace was here. And my entire career I actually worked in various locations, various shops in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with a letter R?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What part of town is this? What is characteristic of this part?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, I worked in town, downtown. It was the largest shop there was. It was called the Hipermarket. So this is the urban area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant. What I wanted to ask you, in geographical term, what would be the closest feature, natural feature, of the town? In other words, which hills were close to this area?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Do you mean where I lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, where you worked.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: I worked in the city centre, in the urban area. So at Mojmilo or Skenderija, I walls worked in a built up area, urban area. There were buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But when you say at Mojmilo, did you work -- was it at Mojmilo hill itself or where?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: No. It was below Mojmilo, Mojmilo hill, but the entire neighbourhood is called Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, the place where you lived, where you were born, how long have you lived there? How long has your family, your ancestors lived there?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: My family has lived here for more than 300 years. You can see the names, place names, Mijatovici, Remezi, Latosi [phoen]. So these are all old families who had moved there a long, long time ago, and we've lived there for 300 years and, actually, we lived there until the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please try and tell us something about one issue. What was the ethnic background of the population living there where your house was? And could you please mark the areas with the predominantly Serb population, but mark it.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: In the area where I lived, it was a predominantly Serb area. From Zuc, from this area here, through Smiljevici, the whole of Zabradze, to the entrance to our village. So this entire area here. And if I may finish, in the Brijesca area, here, these were all Serbs, old families living here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who were your neighbours and where were they? Again, since we have to bring this up, could you please also give us their ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: Well, on this map, you can see this green area here. There are no houses marked here. But in this area here, here, our Muslims neighbours lived. There were about 20.000 of them just before the war. They moved there in 1974 and later; and according to the 1991 census, there were about 20.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what were your relations? Were you on good terms with them until the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: In the village of Smiljevici, there were Muslims and Croats, too. And our relations were impeccable; in other words, people who had lived there for centuries. We were on excellent terms. There were no problems. In the village of Brijesca, there were other Muslims and Croat who had lived there for centuries and we had no problems. But once people started moving in from other areas, problems starting cropping up, primarily because there some tensions. Just before the war broke out, 1991, there was some problems in cafes, all kinds of stories, and this is how things developed until the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Judges in -- very briefly, how the first clashes, minor clashes started breaking out, and how did this evolve into what happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: As I said, we really didn't have any problems with those enemy we had known for years, but some things started happening --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: SINISA KRSMAN
utterances.text: But some things started happening that we simply could not comprehend. First of all, a Serb guest at a wedding was killed at Bascarsija. He was killed only because he was carrying a Serb flag. This was something inconceivable to believe us. And then very close to us, sometime in April, an attack on Boseca Kula happened. I can mark it here, and the Patriotic League and the so-called Green Berets hurled grenades on this gas station. It was owned by a rich man by the name of Bosic from our neighbourhood. The pretext was that some Chetniks had been hiding there at the gas station. Then there was an attack on the Pretis defence industry in Vogosca where, again, the Green Berets attacked the factory and tried to seize some weapons. All this engendered some fear among the people. There was some psychological pressure on the people. People were upset, especially in light of the fact that we all had families, children, and we were all so upset that we didn't know what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's time for the break. So we'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just save this so we don't lose this marked copy of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be saved. We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
